subject: Architecture
title: Babylonian Walls and the Ishtar Gate
description: A micro-lesson that makes Babylonian Walls and the Ishtar Gate usable.

hook.text: Babylon's walls were so thick that chariots could race on top of them — side by side.

buildup.text: King Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon with glazed blue-brick walls decorated with golden animals.

discovery.text: The Ishtar Gate displayed 575 dragons and bulls in glazed tile — each one individually molded and fired.

twist.text: German archaeologists dismantled the gate in 1902 and shipped it to Berlin. Iraq wants it back.

climax.text: Babylon's Processional Way was lined with 120 lion reliefs — worshippers walked through a corridor of beasts.

punchline.text: The gate is in Berlin. The dragons still guard a road that no longer exists.

quiz.question: How many animals were depicted on the Ishtar Gate?

details.summary: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, built around 575 BCE under Nebuchadnezzar II, was covered in brilliant blue glazed bricks depicting lions, bulls, and dragons. Part of a massive double wall system, it was one of the ancient world's most impressive urban fortifications and ceremonial entrances.
details.whyItMatters: The Ishtar Gate shows that ancient architecture served propaganda as well as defense. Its dazzling decoration announced Babylonian power to every visitor entering the city through its ceremonial processional way.
takeaways: The Ishtar Gate featured blue glazed bricks with animal reliefs
Built around 575 BCE under Nebuchadnezzar II
It served both defensive and ceremonial propaganda purposes

faq.question: Where is the Ishtar Gate today?
faq.answer: The reconstructed gate stands in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, assembled from original glazed bricks excavated in the early 1900s. A smaller replica stands at the entrance to the archaeological site in modern Iraq.

faq.question: How were the blue glazed bricks made?
faq.answer: Babylonian craftsmen applied a cobalt and copper-based glaze to molded bricks before firing them in kilns at high temperatures. The technique produced a vivid lapis-lazuli blue that has survived over 2,500 years largely intact.
